Corporate competitors, certainly. But are they "ignorant" or just evil?

I'm not really favoring the word "evil." I like selfish more. It's tangible and removes any "religious" component to the conversation and adds more responsibility. But I'm not sure it would apply to this quote or not.

As an atheist I, for some time, stopped using the word "evil" as well. I've started using it again after considering that its best definition comes from its opposite "good".

What is "good" became the central goal of the Stoics and Cynics of ancient Greece and Rome. The Golden Rule, the cornerstone of ethics (treat others and you would want to be treated/Rule of Reciprocity) could be said to be a secondary reflection of pursuing what felt to be morally "good". What you feel to be "good" is the innate sense of the moral good. Good springs from one's intentions, from one's motivations.

Evil, on the other hand, is the indulgence, desire, and ultimately, ignorance. In this way, no action can be inherently "evil" or "good" as it is the intention or lack of understanding, perhaps of one's self, that leads to "evil".

In Buddhism, too, there is this dichotomy. Good oft equates to the state of mind of calm and contentment, serenity which springs from the healthy mind, the mind that is mindful and not driven by "selfish" or unmindful instincts of greed, jealousy, anger, etc. Ultimately, mindfulness leads to serenity and good intentions, compassion and away from "evil" impulses.

Clearly, there is a great overlap here. Both schools of thought are essentially experiential takes on good-evil and morality. Emphasis is on the inner working that lead to outward action. Buddhism maybe has more emphasis on the use of meditative practice/nothingness to achieve mindfulness compared to the Western contemplative traditions but they both arrive at the same place for all intents and purposes.

Which, in my mind, makes the Cynic/Stoic/Buddhist just philosophical schools of thought and practice rather than religious undertakings. And the use of Good/Evil are thus philosophical terms, not religious ones.

In neither the Western Cynic/Stoic understanding or the Eastern/Buddhist understanding do these considerations form a truly "religious" practice, a practice set around dogmatic dictates and absolutes. (Yes, Buddhism does have branches that have dogmatic and mythical elements that are truly religious and culturally dictated, not just philosophical but the core is still philosophical).

So I am feeling pretty comfortable now with the use of "evil" and "good" from my atheist view point.
I always hope this holds true when I encounter opposition to my opinions.
